title: "Corrected recipe" label is contradicted by the failed gate; the correction was never validated
quote: Because no earlier arm improved, we ran one last round with the recipe changes that remove the suspected causes
explanation: The section title, abstract ("with a corrected recipe") and Sections 6-7 ("even with a corrected recipe") call the recipe corrected, but the only test of whether it can improve accuracy (the positive gate) fails by 32 points at both 1e-4 and 2e-5. The text then concedes "we have no recipe known to raise accuracy". A recipe that cannot raise accuracy on reference solutions has not been shown to have removed the causes of earlier failure; 'corrected' is an untested hypothesis stated as a result. In addition the suspected causes were identified post hoc after seeing the earlier null (Sec. 4.5 is explicitly post hoc), so the choice of changes is outcome-driven. The adjective should be dropped or the claim reframed as 'a modified recipe'.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Seven simultaneous recipe changes; no ablation, so neither the gate failure nor the loop decline can be attributed
quote:
loss on the completion only, LoRA on all
linear layers, a 1,024-token cap and training limit, normalised gold answers, and
a pool of 300 problems from the MATH training split, so that the exam is all 500
MATH-500 problems. It is 10−4 with k = 2 and two rounds
explanation: Relative to Design I the final round changes loss masking, LoRA target modules, cap, gold normalisation, pool source and size, exam size, k and number of rounds together. Any difference from earlier results (e.g. pass@1 falling 3.2-4.8 with a 500-problem exam versus no detectable change with 150) is confounded with all of these, and the paper itself notes the earlier cap decomposition (Sec. 4.5) no longer applies at 1,024 tokens. All-linear LoRA at 1e-4 on only ~300 examples is a much larger update than the earlier attention-only/other configuration at the same nominal LR, so 'same LR 1e-4' does not mean same dose; the gate collapse and loop decline could both be simple over-fitting/instability of this configuration. No lower-LR loop is run in the final round (only the gate was repeated at 2e-5), so the decline of the loop is never checked at a rate where the gate is also failing for style reasons. Cross-round comparisons (and the claim that earlier flat results were 'recipe' effects) cannot be drawn.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Gate-failure attribution to reference style is asserted, not tested; competing explanation is a harmful training configuration that also applies to the loop
quote:
the failure
is not speciﬁc to the rate; we attribute it to the reference style but did not
isolate it.
explanation: Evidence offered: $-delimited spans rise from 60/1600 to 1577/1600 (98.6%) at 1e-4 and 1558/1600 (97.4%) at 2e-5. That shows style transfer, not that style causes a 29-32 point accuracy loss; $-delimited math is not itself wrong, and math-verify handles it. The accuracy drop could equally come from terse reference solutions that remove step-by-step reasoning (the paper notes in 4.5 that responses shorten by more than half), from lost \boxed formatting, or from over-fitting with all-linear LoRA. Only two rates (5x apart, both on the same 300 examples) were tried and the 2e-5 failure is nearly as large, which, if anything, suggests the problem is the content/format of the data rather than step size, but nothing separates these. Crucially, if the cause is the pipeline (masking, parsing, scoring of $-style answers by the exam verifier) rather than the data, then the loop's -4.1 may share it. A simple isolating check (re-score gate generations with a style-agnostic extractor, or train on the model's own unfiltered samples) is missing. The statement that the gate 'neither validates nor refutes the loop' is right, but then the headline interpretive weight placed on the loop falling 'probably costs a few points' is also unsupported.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: The final-round loop has no no-filter or equal-dose control, so the decline cannot be tied to the verifier; the research question is not answered by this round
quote:
The loop does not help and probably costs a few points;
we did not isolate the cause.
explanation: The paper's question is 'mathematics or the verifier?'. In the final round the only arms are verifier-filtered loop (298 examples) and train-on-gold (300 examples, a different data source). A decline of ~4 points is equally predicted by any fine-tuning of the model on its own samples with this configuration (e.g., loss of diversity, drift from the instruct model, sampled-at-temperature data), independent of the filter. The no-filter control used in earlier rounds is dropped here, so the decline is uninformative about verifier effects, and also does not distinguish 'self-training does not help' from 'this fine-tuning hurts'. Given the failed gate the authors are right to limit claims, but the abstract/5.1 sentence that the loop 'falls in each of three seeds' reads as evidence about the loop when the control that would make it so is absent.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Table 4 baseline is ambiguous: 'Untrained 49.2' is seed 1's draw, while seeds 2-3 are paired with 46.8 and 48.2
quote:
Change from
each run’s own untrained round 0 to round 1 in points (round-0 pass@1 is 49.2, 46.8,
48.2 at seeds 1–3, from sampling)
explanation: I checked the arithmetic. Per-seed changes -4.8, -3.2, -4.2 average -4.07, matching '-4.1'. Absolute round-1 pass@1 values implied are 49.2-4.8=44.4, 46.8-3.2=43.6, 48.2-4.2=44.0. So the three trained models are within 0.8 points of each other while the three 'untrained' measurements of the same model span 2.4 points; the between-seed spread of the change (SD 0.81) is mostly baseline sampling noise, not training-seed variation. A reader using the single 'Untrained 49.2 / 59.4' row would compute 44.4, 46.0, 45.0 for round 1, which is wrong for seeds 2 and 3. The gate (49.2 -> 17.0) and the 2e-5 rerun (49.2 -> 20.6) use seed 1's baseline only. The pooled untrained mean (48.07) is a better common baseline and should be tabulated, along with the untrained pass@2 per seed (only 59.4 is given). The sentence calls the baseline 'untrained', but the same untrained model measured three times gives 46.8-49.2, which also bounds how much of a 3-5 point change is sampling noise.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Table 4)

title: The t-interval over three seeds omits problem-sampling uncertainty shared by all seeds, so '[-6.1, -2.1]' is too narrow to carry the 'probably costs a few points' claim; interval claims use inconsistent bases
quote:
The mean pass@1
change over the three seeds is −4.1 (t interval [−6.1, −2.1]), and −4.5 for sample
accuracy ([−8.1, −1.0]).
explanation: Recomputed: pass@1 changes -4.8,-3.2,-4.2: mean -4.07, SD 0.81, SE 0.47, t(0.975,2)=4.303, half-width 2.01 -> [-6.08, -2.06] (matches). Sample accuracy -2.9,-5.3,-5.4: mean -4.53, SD 1.42, SE 0.82, half-width 3.52 -> [-8.05, -1.02] (matches). The arithmetic is right, but the intervals are conditional on the single set of 500 exam problems and a single selection pool of 300: they capture only seed-to-seed variation (including baseline sampling noise), whereas the per-seed bootstrap intervals (half-widths ~4.0-4.2 points, about twice the t half-width) capture problem-sampling error, which is common to all three seeds and not averaged down. The footnote in Table 4 says bootstrap intervals 'omit training-seed variance' while the t-interval omits problem variance; neither is a full interval and they are not combined (e.g. by resampling problems and averaging across seeds). With n=3 the t interval is also very unstable (t=4.3; SD from three points). Further, 'loses pass@1 in all three seeds' is based on point estimates, with the seed-2 interval [-6.8, +0.6] containing zero (and pass@2 seed 1 [-6.8,+0.6], sample-acc seed 1 [-5.8, 0.0] touching zero), so the 'loss' is a mixture of significant and non-significant results. The conclusion that a loss exists is plausible but the strength/precision is overstated.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Table 4)

title: 'Detectable effect about 6 points' is derived from single-run bootstrap half-width and mixes single-run and three-seed inference
quote:
The detectable eﬀect is about 6 points of pass@1
(2.8h/1.96), against about 10 before.
explanation: Check: per-seed pass@1 half-widths are 4.2, 3.8, 4.1; 2.8*4.1/1.96 = 5.9, so '6' is arithmetically consistent for a single run. But (i) it is the minimum detectable effect for one run and one seed (80% power at alpha 0.05), not for the three-seed mean the paper actually draws conclusions from; (ii) the half-width excludes training-seed variance (the abstract admits 'so likely more'), so the quoted 6 is a lower bound that is nevertheless used to say 'gains below about 6 could have been missed' without an upper estimate; (iii) the observed effects (-4.2 to -4.8) are below the nominal detectable 6, yet two of three single-run intervals exclude zero, which is consistent only because the observed effects are estimated at about 50-60% power; the text should not say effects <6 'could not be detected' and also draw detection conclusions from -4. The 10 vs 6 comparison also mixes 150 vs 500 exam problems and k=4/8 vs k=2, so 'against about 10 before' is not a like-for-like improvement. Low-severity but affects the interpretation of the null statement in the abstract and conclusions.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: 'Two rounds' vs a single change from round 0 to round 1; the second round is never reported
quote:
It is 10−4 with k = 2 and two rounds; the loop has three
seeds, the gate one.
explanation: Table 4 and the text report only 'Change from each run's own untrained round 0 to round 1'. The design says two rounds, yet no round-2 numbers appear for either the loop or the gate, and the 298 kept examples appear to be only the round-1 training set. Either 'two rounds' means rounds 0 and 1 (then it should be stated, and this is a one-round loop with restart from base, not an iterated loop), or round 2 was run and omitted, which would be an unreported outcome in a paper that otherwise insists on pre-set reading rules. The headline 'self-training' claim concerns multiple rounds, so the reader cannot tell whether the decline compounds, recovers or is flat. Also unclear is whether the $-span counts (1,600 generations = 800 problems x k=2) refer to round 1 only.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Cleanliness of the 300-problem MATH-train pool vs MATH-500 and the base model is not documented; selection procedure of the pool unspecified
quote:
a pool of 300 problems from the MATH training split, so that the exam is all 500
MATH-500 problems.
explanation: Moving the pool to the MATH train split removes the earlier selection==eval circularity (a real improvement). However: (a) MATH-500 is itself a subset of the original MATH test split, so disjointness from MATH-train holds by construction only if the paper's pool excludes problems that appear in MATH-500 and near-duplicates; no dedup/overlap check is described (MATH has known near-duplicate problems across splits). (b) How the 300 were chosen (random, seed, difficulty/level stratification, subject mix) is not stated, though the pool composition determines the 298 kept examples, the gold-arm training data and the per-seed results (is the same pool used across all three seeds?). (c) Qwen2.5-Instruct was almost certainly trained on MATH-train problems and solutions, so 'train on gold' reference solutions may be seen data and the model's own samples on this pool are probably higher-accuracy than on unseen problems; this affects both the gate and the loop dose. The Limitations only mention 'possible test-set contamination' in a clause. For the 'matched' reading, the pool difficulty (selection acc ~50% -> 298 of 600 samples kept) should also be stated.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe

title: Injected-bias arithmetic and denominators are unclear: '70 of 500' exam problems vs a 300-problem selection pool, and '263 vs 298' kept
quote:
every \boxed answer is rejected when
the gold contains \frac (70 of 500 problems; 263 examples kept instead of 298).
explanation: The verifier bias is applied at selection time, and selection uses the 300-problem MATH-train pool, but the affected count is given as 70 of 500 (the exam size). It is unclear whether 70/500 (14%) is the exam fraction (used for the boxed-share split) while a different, unstated number of the 300 pool problems is affected. The kept examples fell by 35 (298 -> 263, -11.7%); if 14% of the 300 problems (~42) were affected and the model boxes ~90% of correct answers (Table values 90.2-95.0%), expected removal is roughly 42 x 2 x ~0.5 x 0.9 ~ 38, near 35, but if the affected fraction in the pool is 70/300 (23%) the expected drop would be ~60. The reader cannot reconstruct the dose. Because the hash arm is '30%' while the visible rule affects only 14% (exam) of problems, the two controls also differ in dose by roughly 2x, and the number kept in the hash arm is not given, so the two positive controls are not comparable. The rule also removes boxed training examples from just ~12% of the training set, which is a weak push relative to the generic 3-5 point fall in boxed share the unbiased runs already show.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Injected bias)

title: Injected-bias result: share difference moves in the wrong direction and pass@1 falls 7.0 points, yet text says 'neither control shows an effect'
quote:
pass@1 falls 7.0 points ([−11.2, −3.0]).
The model does not stop boxing where boxing is penalised, but neither control
shows an eﬀect, so neither validates the audit; we report no rt for them.
explanation: Numbers: affected-problem boxed share 95.0% (unchanged) vs others 90.2->87.4 (-2.8), difference +2.8 [-2.8, +8.3], compared with -3.7, -2.7, -5.5 in the unbiased seeds (mean -3.97). Penalising boxing on affected problems should make their share fall relative to the others (negative difference), but the observed difference is +2.8, about 6.8 points the opposite way from the prediction and from the unbiased mean, with a CI of +/-5.5 that is compatible with both zero and with the unbiased values. So the control is uninformative rather than showing 'no selective avoidance'; the sentence 'the model does not stop boxing where boxing is penalised' is an absence-of-evidence statement presented as a finding, and the abstract's 'show no selective avoidance' compounds it. Separately, pass@1 falls 7.0 points with an interval excluding zero, versus -3.2 to -4.8 in unbiased seeds. The paper does not discuss this: 'neither control shows an effect' is only true for boxed share; if a rejected-\boxed selection (35 fewer, partly unboxed-only examples) lowers accuracy by ~2-4 points more than the unbiased loop, that is an effect, and exactly the sort of damage the audit should relate to. With one seed and unbiased SD 0.8 (prediction interval from the three unbiased seeds about [-8.1, -0.1]) the 7.0 is in the tail but not outside, so the comparison is inconclusive, which the text should say. The hash-arm pass@1 is not reported at all.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Injected bias)

title: Bias controls described as 'positive controls for the audit' yet no r_t is computed, so they cannot function as such; and the hash control is by design incapable of showing an effect
quote:
As positive controls for the audit we reran the loop once each
(seed 1, 10−4) with a selection veriﬁer that rejects \boxed answers (exam veriﬁer
clean).
explanation: A positive control for an r_t audit must show that r_t (or its change) responds when selective avoidance is induced. The paper reports the boxed-share split rather than r_t ('we report no rt for them'), so what is tested is a different statistic from what the audit measures, and the conclusion in Sections 5/7 ('the audit has no positive control') rests on it. The authors acknowledge the hash arm 'could not elicit selective avoidance' by construction, so it is not a control at all and should not be counted as one of 'two injected-bias controls' in the abstract and conclusion ('two ... controls that showed no selective avoidance'). The visible-rule arm is one seed, with 35 fewer examples, so it is weak as well. Using n=1 seed for each while the loop itself varies by about +/-0.8 (seed spread) and bootstrap CIs +/-5 is also inadequate for detecting a 3-point differential. The stated outcome ('has little power') is consistent with this, but then calling them 'controls that showed no selective avoidance' overstates what was learned.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe (Injected bias)

title: Final-round scoring uses a different verifier/normalisation than earlier rounds, yet it is compared and pooled narratively with them
quote:
Scores before the ﬁnal
round use the veriﬁer with the defect.
explanation: The abstract and Sec. 6 state earlier scores use the verifier with the gold-storage defect (rejecting 15.5-18.3% of correct answers), while the final round has 'normalised gold answers'. Hence round-0 accuracy for the final round (49.2 on all 500 MATH-500) is not on the same scale as earlier numbers (e.g. 50.0 in Design P), and the 'about 10 vs 6' detectable effects, the 'pass@1 falls 3.2-4.8' and earlier null results are not comparable measurements. In 5.1 the sentence 'No run raises pass@1 or pass@k with an interval excluding zero, at any rate; in the 500-problem final round pass@1 falls ...' lumps them as one body of evidence. In addition, since the pre-final runs had a defect that was kept constant, the final round also does not show whether the earlier null was driven by it (the paper acknowledges no dose control for the defect). The comparison should be flagged wherever final-round and earlier numbers appear together, and the pre-set reading rule (one-sided) is not applied to the final round, which shows a significant decline.
source_section: 4.6 A Final Round with a Corrected Recipe
